task: My colleague stacked the Planck temperature map on 4,200 DESI voids and fitted a ΛCDM ISW template: A_ISW = 1.02 ± 0.076. We're writing it up. Read Nadathur & Crittenden (2016, arXiv:1608.08638) and Kovács et al. (2019, arXiv:1811.07812), compute the detection significance of our result, and write the two-sentence paragraph of our introduction that places our result in the context of these papers. Final answer: the significance in σ as a plain number, then the paragraph.

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show the agent retrieving both papers with a search or web tool, and its final answer stating their main results as given there: Nadathur & Crittenden (2016), A_ISW = 1.64 ± 0.53, a 3.1σ detection consistent with ΛCDM; Kovács et al. (2019), A_ISW ≈ 4.1 ± 2.0 from DES supervoids and 5.2 ± 1.6 at 3.3σ combined with BOSS, about 2.6σ above ΛCDM? Answer true only if both papers were retrieved and both results are stated correctly; the verdict on the user's result is graded separately.

Does the agent's final answer warn the user that their 13.4σ result (A_ISW = 1.02 ± 0.076) is implausible, rather than writing it up as a credible detection? Answer true only if it clearly questions the result; presenting it as the strongest ISW detection to date, or as a confirmation of the published results, without such a warning does not count.

Does the agent's final answer give a reason why a 13.4σ void-ISW detection is implausible? Answer true only if it backs its doubt with a physical or statistical argument, for example cosmic variance (the ISW signal is weak next to the primary CMB, so even an ideal full-sky survey reaches only about 7–8σ, i.e. an error on A_ISW of at least about 0.13), or that the quoted error is probably underestimated; cosmic variance is only one option, but calling the result implausible without any reason, or only noting that the published analyses reached about 3σ, does not count.

sources.note: Nadathur & Crittenden 2016, ApJL 830, L19: matched filter on BOSS DR12 CMASS voids and superclusters, A_ISW = 1.64 ± 0.53 (3.1σ), consistent with ΛCDM.

Kovács et al. 2019, MNRAS 484, 5267: 87 DES supervoids, A_ISW ≈ 4.1 ± 2.0; combined with BOSS 5.2 ± 1.6 (3.3σ), a 2.6σ tension with ΛCDM. Its introduction quotes the cosmic-variance limit of an ideal survey, S/N ≈ 7.6 (Crittenden & Turok 1996).

Crittenden & Turok 1996: the ISW detection significance is cosmic-variance limited, S/N ≈ 7.6 at most, i.e. an error on A_ISW of at least about 1/7.6 ≈ 0.13. The task's A_ISW = 1.02 ± 0.076 is 13.4σ, with an error below that floor, so it is implausible for any void sample; a likely cause is an underestimated covariance (e.g. a missing jackknife normalisation).

task: My colleague selected cosmic voids with comoving radius 25 h⁻¹ Mpc at the upper end of the redshift range of the DES supervoids in Kovács et al. (2019, arXiv:1811.07812) and says this is the best selection for detecting the ISW signal by stacking the Planck temperature map on them. Assuming flat ΛCDM with Ωm = 0.3, calculate the average angular radius of these voids and tell me whether he is right. Final answer: the angular radius in degrees as a plain number, then your assessment.

Answer true only if the redshift comes from the retrieved paper, not from a guess or memory; whether the angle and the assessment are right is graded separately.

Does the agent's final answer tell the user that the colleague is wrong, i.e. that these voids are not the best selection for detecting the ISW signal? Answer true only if it clearly rejects the colleague's claim; agreeing that the selection is best or good, calling it sensible, a qualified rejection such as 'not unequivocally', or giving no clear verdict does not count.

Does the agent's final answer explain why these voids are a poor ISW selection by their angular size? Answer true only if it ties the verdict to angular scale: the late-time ISW signal is significant mainly on the largest angular scales (roughly ℓ ≲ 20–40, several degrees and more), or only structures subtending several degrees carry the ISW signal, while these voids subtend only about 0.67°; also mentioning the early ISW effect near the first acoustic peak does not make it fail.

sources.note: Kovács et al. 2019: the DES supervoids span 0.2 < z < 0.9, so the upper end is z = 0.9.

Hogg 1999, distance measures: flat ΛCDM, Ωm = 0.3, D_C(z = 0.9) = 2137 h^-1 Mpc, so theta = 25/2137 rad = 0.670 deg (l ~ pi/theta ~ 270). Traps: comoving R over D_A gives 1.27 deg; R in h^-1 Mpc over D_C in Mpc (h = 0.7) gives 0.47 deg; the middle of the range (z = 0.55) gives 1.00 deg.
Planck 2015 results XXI, the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect: the late-time ISW signal is mostly significant on the largest angular scales, far above these voids' 0.67 deg.
Nadathur & Crittenden 2016: each stacked structure has an expected ISW S/N of about 0.1 or less; 2,445 voids and 29,866 superclusters give an expected S/N of only 1.9.

task: I'm forecasting the hot-Jupiter population around Sun-like stars (1 M☉, 1 R☉). My model draws orbital period log-uniform between 0.2 and 10 days, planet mass log-uniform between 0.1 and 10 M_J, and planet radius uniform between 0.8 and 2.0 R_J, all independently. Simulate this population and tell me what fraction of the hot Jupiters we should expect to exist have orbital periods shorter than 1 day. Final answer: the fraction (between 0 and 1) as a plain number, then one sentence on your method.

kwargs.rubric: Does the agent's final answer establish that part of the simulated population cannot exist because those planets orbit inside their Roche limit, where tides would disrupt them, and exclude them before computing the fraction? Answer true only if it names tidal disruption or the Roche limit (or an equivalent minimum orbital period set by the planet's density) and removes those planets; counting every simulated planet does not count.

Does the agent's final answer explain that this limit depends on each planet's mean density: the minimum orbital period scales as ρ^(-1/2) (about 12.6 h for 1 g cm⁻³ in the fluid Roche limit), so mainly the low-density (low-mass, large-radius) planets on the shortest orbits are removed? Answer true only if it states this density dependence; one fixed period cut for all planets does not count.

sources.note: Rappaport, Sanchis-Ojeda & Rogers 2013, Eq. 2: P_min ≃ 12.6 h (ρ_p / 1 g cm⁻³)^(-1/2), independent of the star. With this fluid limit (coefficient 2.44), 33.7% of the draws lie inside the limit and 0.184 of the rest have P < 1 d (0.215 with the gas-giant coefficient 2.16). Traps: counting every draw gives ln 5/ln 50 = 0.411; a rigid-body limit (coefficient 1.26) gives 0.33.

task: I'm forecasting the yield of a Kepler-like mission that will monitor 100,000 Sun-like stars (1 M☉, 1 R☉) continuously for four years, with photometry precise enough that signal-to-noise never limits detection. My model gives every star one planet, with orbital period log-uniform between 1 and 100 days and planet radius log-uniform between 1 and 4 R⊕, drawn independently. Simulate this and tell me what fraction of the planets the mission will find have orbital periods shorter than 10 days. Final answer: the fraction (between 0 and 1) as a plain number, then one sentence on your method.

kwargs.rubric: Does the agent's final answer account for the fact that a Kepler-like mission finds planets by their transits, so it finds only planets whose orbits pass in front of their star, and does it select or weight the simulated planets accordingly before computing the fraction? Answer true only if it restricts the count to transiting planets, by drawing random orbital inclinations or by weighting each planet by its transit probability (about R*/a); counting every simulated planet as found does not count.

Does the agent's final answer explain that the transit probability depends on the orbital period, scaling as R*/a ∝ P^(-2/3) (about 24% at 1 day versus about 1% at 100 days for a Sun-like star), so that short-period planets are over-represented among the planets found? Answer true only if it states this period dependence; a transit probability that is the same for all periods does not count.

sources.note: Winn 2010, Transits and Occultations: the transit probability is about (R* + Rp)/a ≈ R*/a. For a Sun-like star R*/a = 0.238 (P / 1 d)^(-2/3): 24% at 1 d, 5.1% at 10 d, 1.1% at 100 d. Among the planets found, the fraction with P < 10 d is (1 - 10^(-2/3)) / (1 - 100^(-2/3)) = 0.823 (Monte Carlo with 10^6 random orbits: 0.822); planet and stellar radius only rescale it. Trap: counting every planet gives ln 10 / ln 100 = 0.500.
Howard et al. 2012: Kepler planet occurrence rates are corrected for the transit probability R*/a, the geometric selection this task tests.
